slides.title: Programming foundations
slides.body:
Short revision
Programming Logic and Design
Lefa Malatji

slides.title: Programs, algorithms and quality
points: A computer follows instructions to process data. Hardware is physical equipment. Software consists of programs and supporting data.
An algorithm is a finite set of unambiguous steps for solving a problem. A program implements those steps in a language.
Quality includes correctness, readable names, validation and tests. Test typical, boundary and invalid input.

slides.title: Program development life cycle
points: 1. Analyse the problem: identify inputs, required outputs and constraints.
2. Design the algorithm with pseudocode, diagrams and test cases.
3. Implement the design and test the results against expectations.
4. Document, maintain and improve the program after release.

slides.title: Data types and storage
rows: INTEGER requires whole values. REAL accepts decimals too.
Text such as "Lebo" / TRUE or FALSE
A variable can change. A constant keeps its value.
slides.note: Declare names before use. Give a value before reading a variable in an expression.

slides.title: Worked example: input and calculation
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE price AS NUM
  DECLARE quantity AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS NUM
  INPUT price
  INPUT quantity
  SET total = price * quantity
  OUTPUT total
END
points: Inputs: price = 12.5 and quantity = 3.
Calculation: 12.5 * 3 = 37.5.
Output: 37.5. A type check alone does not reject a negative quantity. A business rule must do that.

slides.title: Operators and precedence
rows: Compare first, then NOT, then AND, then OR.
slides.note: 2 + 3 * 4 = 14. (2 + 3) * 4 = 20. DIV gives a truncated quotient. MOD gives the corresponding remainder.

slides.title: Pseudocode and flowchart symbols
points: Pseudocode expresses logic in readable steps. This course uses BEGIN, DECLARE, INPUT, SET and OUTPUT.
The chart calculates one more than the input.
Rounded terminals show start/end. Parallelograms show input/output. Rectangles show declarations and calculations.

slides.title: Control structures and tracing
rows: Choose a branch using a Boolean condition.
Repeat statements while a rule permits.
Record variable values and output after each step.
slides.note: A trace follows actual execution. An untaken branch does not change the state.

slides.title: Practice and worked answer
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE total AS NUM = 5
  SET total = total + 2
  SET total = total * 3
  OUTPUT total
END
points: Question: What is the output? Write the value after each assignment.
Answer: total starts at 5, becomes 7, then becomes 21. Output is 21.
Question: Why is OUTPUT not an assignment? Answer: it displays the current value without replacing it.

slides.title: Common mistakes and final checks
points: Undeclared or unassigned values: declare the variable and assign or input a value before reading it.
Incorrect calculation order: apply precedence or use parentheses.
Missing validation: a valid numeric type can still contain an unacceptable value.
Before finishing: trace one normal case, one boundary case and one invalid case.

slides.title: Decisions and loops
slides.body:
Short revision
Programming Logic and Design
Lefa Malatji

slides.title: Boolean expressions
rows: TRUE when mark is at least 50.
At least one condition must be TRUE.
slides.note: Comparisons bind before NOT, then AND, then OR. Parentheses make complex intent clear.

slides.title: Worked selection: IF and ELSE
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE mark AS NUM = 50
  IF mark >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Pass"
  ELSE
    OUTPUT "Revise"
  ENDIF
END
points: At mark = 50, the condition is TRUE and output is Pass.
At mark = 49, output is Revise.
Nested IF places a second decision inside a branch. ELSEIF tests another condition after an earlier FALSE result.

slides.title: Worked selection: SWITCH
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE option AS INTEGER = 2
  SWITCH option
    CASE 1:
      OUTPUT "Add"
    CASE 2:
      OUTPUT "View"
    DEFAULT:
      OUTPUT "Invalid option"
  ENDSWITCH
END
points: The output is View.
SWITCH selects a branch by matching a value. DEFAULT handles unmatched values.
This pseudocode dialect executes the selected case without fall-through.

slides.title: Worked FOR loop and accumulator
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS NUM = 0
  FOR i = 1 TO 3
    SET total = total + i
  ENDFOR
  OUTPUT total
END
points: An accumulator stores a running result. Initialise total before the loop.

i = 1: total becomes 1.
i = 2: total becomes 3.
i = 3: total becomes 6.
Both bounds are inclusive. Output is 6. A negative STEP can count down.

slides.title: Worked WHILE loop and priming input
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE value AS NUM
  DECLARE total AS NUM = 0
  INPUT value
  WHILE value <> -1 DO
    SET total = total + value
    INPUT value
  ENDWHILE
  OUTPUT total
END
points: The first INPUT is the priming input. It gives the condition an initial value.
-1 is a sentinel that ends input and is not added.
Inputs 10, 20, -1 produce output 30. A first input of -1 produces 0.

slides.title: Worked REPEAT loop
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE mark AS NUM
  REPEAT
    INPUT mark
  UNTIL mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100
  OUTPUT mark
END
points: REPEAT tests after its body, so input happens at least once.
Inputs 120, -5, 70 cause three attempts. The final condition is TRUE for 70.
UNTIL TRUE ends the loop. WHILE TRUE continues its loop.

slides.title: Nested loops
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE row AS INTEGER
  DECLARE column AS INTEGER
  FOR row = 0 TO 1
    FOR column = 0 TO 2
      OUTPUT row, column
    ENDFOR
  ENDFOR
END
points: The inner loop completes for each outer iteration.
2 rows * 3 columns = 6 executions of OUTPUT.

slides.title: Practice and worked answers
points: Question: A loop starts at count = 1, displays count and increments it while count <= 3. What appears?
Answer: 1, then 2, then 3. count becomes 4 and the next condition is FALSE.
Question: What changes if count decreases by 1 instead?
Answer: count keeps satisfying count <= 3. The loop does not terminate unless another rule stops it.

slides.title: Common mistakes and final checks
points: A boundary error excludes or includes one value too many. Test the exact threshold.
A loop without a useful update may never end. A counter must move toward termination.
Reset an accumulator only where the intended group begins.
Before finishing: test zero iterations, one iteration and repeated iterations. REPEAT always runs its body at least once.

slides.title: Arrays and algorithms
slides.body:
Short revision
Programming Logic and Design
Lefa Malatji

slides.title: Array essentials
rows: A collection of values accessed by index.
Allocation alone leaves each element unassigned.
slides.note: A read needs an assigned element. Array sizes and indexes must be whole numbers.

slides.title: Worked array update
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE values[3] AS NUM
  SET values[0] = 2
  SET values[1] = 5
  SET values[2] = 8
  SET values[1] = values[0] + values[2]
  OUTPUT values[1]
END
points: Before the last assignment: [2, 5, 8].
values[1] becomes 2 + 8 = 10.
After: [2, 10, 8]. Output is 10.

slides.title: Input and total with a loop
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE values[3] AS NUM
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS NUM = 0
  FOR i = 0 TO 2
    INPUT values[i]
    SET total = total + values[i]
  ENDFOR
  OUTPUT total
END
points: Inputs 2, 3 and 4 fill indexes 0, 1 and 2.
The accumulator becomes 2, then 5, then 9.
Output is 9. The final valid index is length minus 1.

slides.title: Two-dimensional arrays
slides.code:
BEGIN
  DECLARE grid[2][3] AS NUM
  DECLARE row AS INTEGER
  DECLARE column AS INTEGER
  FOR row = 0 TO 1
    FOR column = 0 TO 2
      INPUT grid[row][column]
    ENDFOR
  ENDFOR
END
points: The first index is the row. The second is the column.
A 2 by 3 grid contains 6 cells. Rows range from 0 to 1 and columns from 0 to 2.

slides.title: Worked linear search
slides.code:
DECLARE values[3] AS NUM
DECLARE i AS INTEGER
DECLARE foundAt AS INTEGER = -1
DECLARE target AS NUM = 8
SET values[0] = 2
SET values[1] = 5
SET values[2] = 8
FOR i = 0 TO 2
  IF values[i] = target THEN
    SET foundAt = i
  ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT foundAt
points: Compare each element with the target.
2 does not match. 5 does not match. 8 matches at index 2. Output is 2.
-1 means not found. This complete scan returns the last matching index when duplicates exist.

slides.title: Parallel arrays
slides.note: For selected = 1, names[selected] is Neo and marks[selected] is 72. When sorting or moving records, move all related array values together.

slides.title: Worked bubble-sort comparison
slides.code:
DECLARE values[2] AS NUM
DECLARE temp AS NUM
SET values[0] = 8
SET values[1] = 3
IF values[0] > values[1] THEN
  SET temp = values[0]
  SET values[0] = values[1]
  SET values[1] = temp
ENDIF
OUTPUT values[0], values[1]
points: 8 > 3 is TRUE. temp stores 8 before it is overwritten.
The pair changes from [8, 3] to [3, 8].
Full bubble sort repeats adjacent comparisons over passes. Each pass places the largest remaining value at the end of its range.

slides.title: Practice and worked answers
points: Question: For an array of length 4, is index 4 valid? Answer: no. The valid indexes are 0 through 3.
Question: How many inputs fill a 3 by 2 grid? Answer: 6 inputs.
Question: Searching [7, 2, 9] for 2 gives which index? Answer: index 1.
Question: Why use a temporary value in a swap? Answer: it preserves one value while the other position changes.

slides.title: Common mistakes and final checks
points: Starting at index 1 skips the first element in a zero-based array.
Using <= length accesses one position beyond the end. Use the last index, length - 1.
Sorting only one parallel array can attach a mark to the wrong learner.
Before finishing: test first/last positions, missing targets, duplicates and an already sorted list.

slides.title: Methods and modules
slides.body:
Short revision
Programming Logic and Design
Lefa Malatji

slides.title: Definitions and method contracts
rows: A named unit that performs a focused task.
An input name declared in the method header.
An actual value supplied at a call.
Required inputs, result and any changes the method makes.
slides.note: A returning method sends data back with RETURN. A method without a return value may perform output or another action.

slides.title: Decomposition and a hierarchy chart
points: Main coordinates the program. Its child modules each handle one responsibility.
A hierarchy chart shows which modules call others. It does not show the timing of decisions or loop iterations.
ReadValues gathers inputs, CalculateTotal computes the result, and DisplayResult presents it.

slides.title: Method without parameters
slides.code:
METHOD showWelcome()
  OUTPUT "Welcome to LogicLab"
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  CALL showWelcome()
END
points: The empty parentheses show that the method requires no parameters.
CALL invokes the method from the main program.
Output: Welcome to LogicLab. Control then returns to the caller.

slides.title: Parameters, arguments and scope
slides.code:
METHOD showDouble(value AS NUM)
  DECLARE doubled AS NUM
  SET doubled = value * 2
  OUTPUT doubled
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  CALL showDouble(4)
END
points: value is a parameter. The argument 4 supplies its initial value.
doubled is local to the method. Its declaration does not create a main-program variable.
Output is 8. OUTPUT displays data without returning it as a result.

slides.title: Worked returning method
slides.code:
METHOD difference(first AS NUM, second AS NUM)
  RETURN first - second
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  DECLARE result AS NUM
  SET result = difference(9, 4)
  OUTPUT result
END
points: first receives 9 and second receives 4.
The method returns 9 - 4 = 5. result receives 5, then OUTPUT displays it.
RETURN ends the current invocation. Statements after an unconditional RETURN cannot execute.

slides.title: Passing an array to a method
slides.code:
METHOD sum(values[] AS NUM, size AS INTEGER)
  DECLARE i AS INTEGER
  DECLARE total AS NUM = 0
  FOR i = 0 TO size - 1
    SET total = total + values[i]
  ENDFOR
  RETURN total
ENDMETHOD
BEGIN
  DECLARE marks[2] AS NUM
  SET marks[0] = 60
  SET marks[1] = 80
  OUTPUT sum(marks, 2)
END
points: values[] declares an array parameter. size states how many assigned elements to process.
The call supplies marks and the size 2. The method adds 60 and 80. Output is 140.
Document whether a method may change the supplied array. This example only reads it.

slides.title: Overloading and call checking
rows: METHOD area(width AS NUM, height AS NUM)
Name plus parameter count and types identifies an overload.
Changing only the return type does not identify a distinct overload.
slides.note: A call must supply the expected number and compatible types of arguments. This table shows headers, not complete method bodies.

slides.title: Practice and worked answers
points: Question: A method returns first - second. What does difference(4, 9) return? Answer: -5.
Question: Can a caller use a local variable declared inside another method? Answer: not directly. Pass data through parameters and return values.
Question: Why split input, calculation and output into modules? Answer: each responsibility becomes easier to test and change.
Method examples are written revision exercises. The live tracer currently executes main-program logic and arrays, rather than method calls.

slides.title: Common mistakes and final checks
points: Confusing OUTPUT with RETURN: a displayed value is not automatically available for assignment by the caller.
Wrong argument count or order: compare the call with its header.
Reading a local variable outside its scope: return the required value or pass it as an input.
Before finishing: test each method with normal and boundary inputs, then test the caller and its dependencies.

slides.title: Object-oriented design
slides.body:
Short revision
Programming Logic and Design
Lefa Malatji

slides.title: Classes, objects and constructors
rows: A blueprint that declares fields and methods.
An instance with its own field values.
Stored state / behaviour that works with state.
Initialises a new object when it is created.
slides.note: NEW creates an object. A reference variable names the object being used. Separate instances normally keep separate instance fields.

slides.title: Access modifiers and encapsulation
rows: Code outside the class can access the member.
Only code in the class can directly access the member.
The class and derived classes can access the member.
Group state and behaviour, and control changes through an interface.
slides.note: These are the course pseudocode conventions. Exact access rules and syntax depend on the implementation language.

slides.title: Worked object state
slides.code:
CLASS Counter
  PRIVATE count AS NUM = 0
  METHOD increment()
    SET count = count + 1
  ENDMETHOD
  METHOD getCount()
    RETURN count
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
points: The private field starts at 0 for each new Counter.
After two increment calls on one object, count is 2. getCount returns 2.
A second new Counter still starts at 0. Its state is independent of the first object.

slides.title: A constructor with a parameter
slides.code:
CLASS Learner
  PRIVATE name AS STRING
  CONSTRUCTOR(newName AS STRING)
    SET name = newName
  ENDCONSTRUCTOR
  METHOD getName()
    RETURN name
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
points: The constructor parameter newName introduces the incoming text.
Creating a Learner with "Neo" stores Neo in name. getName returns Neo.
A constructor establishes a valid initial state. These are design-level examples, not executable tracer syntax.

slides.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
points: Inheritance defines a specialised class from a more general class. Use it for an is-a relationship, such as SavingsAccount is an Account.
A derived class can reuse suitable base behaviour and override a method with a specialised implementation.
Polymorphism lets a call through a common interface select the behaviour of the actual object.
Overriding changes inherited behaviour. Overloading provides different parameter signatures under the same method name.

slides.title: Reading a class diagram
points: A class diagram separates the class name, fields and methods into compartments.
A minus sign means private. A plus sign means public. A hash sign means protected.
balance is private numeric state. deposit accepts a NUM amount. getBalance returns a NUM value.

slides.title: Validation inside a method
slides.code:
CLASS Account
  PRIVATE balance AS NUM = 0
  METHOD deposit(amount AS NUM)
    IF amount > 0 THEN
      SET balance = balance + amount
    ENDIF
  ENDMETHOD
  METHOD getBalance()
    RETURN balance
  ENDMETHOD
ENDCLASS
points: deposit(50) changes balance from 0 to 50.
deposit(-10) leaves the balance at 50 because the condition is FALSE.
The method protects the rule that this deposit operation accepts only positive amounts.

slides.title: Practice and worked answers
points: Question: Is Learner a class or one particular learner? Answer: it is a class. A created Learner object is an instance.
Question: A private field has a value of 5. Does private mean the value can never change? Answer: no. Class methods can change it.
Question: Which relation fits a school containing learners? Answer: has-a, normally modelled with composition or association rather than School inheriting Learner.
Question: What should a class diagram show? Answer: relevant fields, method signatures and relationships with clear visibility.

slides.title: Common mistakes and final checks
points: Confusing class and object: define the blueprint, then identify the instances and their separate state.
Using inheritance for a has-a relationship: model ownership or association explicitly.
Exposing fields without validation can allow invalid state. Decide which changes methods should permit.
Before finishing: check constructor inputs, visibility, field types, method contracts and each required relationship.
